summary:
Jigawa stands under Nigeria's national framework as well as its own state code. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies across the country and, according to Human Rights Watch (October 2016), also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment; police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation and of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity.

Jigawa is one of the twelve northern states that adopted Sharia into their criminal legislation by 2002, a process Human Rights Watch (2004) traces to Zamfara's governor introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000. These twelve states are the only ones where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases. The UK Home Office note states that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Jigawa's own instrument is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed on 18 December 2000 and brought into operation on 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12). The Home Office table for Jigawa gives the penalties as death by stoning for married men, 100 lashes plus imprisonment of up to one year for unmarried men, and same-sex acts between women punished with up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms the code remains in force and that the Sharia penal layer is the operative criminal frame for Muslims in the state.

The state code reaches conduct the federal statute does not supply independently. Its definition of lesbianism carries up to 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment, and Jigawa includes the 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation of the offence — a route to prosecution for women that the federal code, which addresses men's acts, does not provide on its own.

Violence and extraction accompany the legal exposure. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and six months later no suspects had been charged (the Dial, February 2025). TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports a 24-year-old stopped by Lagos police who was struck in the mouth with a gun butt and released only after paying almost half of a 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed: Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), sentenced on 12 April 2024 to six months for naira abuse and held in a maximum-security prison in Lagos until 5 August 2024; press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold her, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion, and an October 2024 panel found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.
tangentialFactors:
Jigawa is one of only four states — alongside Gombe, Kano and Zamfara — whose sodomy offence imposes 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment on unmarried men and stoning to death (rajm) on married men, a penalty pattern shared across a minority of the twelve-state bloc rather than uniform within it.

The twelve-state Sharia layer sits alongside, not instead of, the federal regime. The UK Home Office note directs readers to its section on the Sharia codes in force in Kano, Borno, Kaduna and other northern states (section 8.2.20), and the wider country note records the same federal penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment that apply to visitors in every Nigerian state.

The ten-to-fourteen-year range attached to the federal act reflects Human Rights Watch's reading of the statute; the Home Office figure of up to 14 years is the one carried in official travel and asylum guidance.
localsOnly:
Sharia courts in Jigawa hold criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, a competence confined to the twelve states that legislated it between 1999 and 2002; the state's Law No. 12 of 2000 is the operative text for those prosecutions.

Women resident in the state face exposure under the local code that the federal statute does not independently supply, with lesbianism carrying up to 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment.

The Home Office's June 2025 note is the government confirmation that the state's Sharia penal code remains the operative criminal frame for Muslims in Jigawa.
outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific incident, Hisbah record or court-level study covering Jigawa is present in the source inventory; enforcement rates, arrest frequencies and prosecution outcomes for the state are not sourced here and remain unresolved.

Whether the cross-dressing proposals reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted into law is not settled by the sources available.

The sources do not state whether the Jigawa Sharia Penal Code reaches non-Muslim residents or visitors, or how the state's religious courts interact with federal courts on same-sex offences in practice.

Which prison section holds a trans woman sentenced in Jigawa is not addressed anywhere in the inventory; the placement question is evidenced only by the Bobrisky case in Lagos.
